The words

See where the great incarnate God
Fills a majestic throne,
While from the skies his awful voice
Bears the last judgment down.

"I am the first, and I the last,
"Thro' endless years the same;
"I AM is my memorial still,
"And my eternal name.

"Such favours as a God can give
"My royal grace bestows;
"Ye thirsty souls come taste the streams
"Where life and pleasure flows.

"The saint that triumphs o'er his sins,
"I'll own him for a son,
"The whole creation shall reward
"The conquests he has won.

"But bloody hands and hearts unclean,
"And all the lying race,
"The faithless and the scoffing crew,
"That spurn at offer'd grace,

"They shall be taken from my sight,
"Bound fast in iron chains,
"And headlong plung'd into the lake
"Where fire and darkness reigns."

O may I stand before the Lamb,
When earth and seas are fled!
And hear the Judge pronounce my name
With blessings on my head!

May I with those for ever dwell
Who here were my delight,
While sinners banish'd down to hell,
No more offend my sight.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (D), on the word “See”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for his Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), Book I, collected from the Scriptures, hymn 45, headed “The last judgment, Rev. 21. 5-8”.

Watts' hymns were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Common Metre (8.6.8.6). This page sets the words to CAITHNESS; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Melody (1635): Scottish Psalter

Questions about See Where the Great Incarnate God

What is the doh of See Where the Great Incarnate God?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does See Where the Great Incarnate God start on?

It starts on d (D in D major), a pickup on the word “See” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is See Where the Great Incarnate God in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1635. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
